note.question: When can customers credibly reveal privately known quality preferences during customization, and should the seller elicit those preferences directly or delegate product design to customers?
note.overview: The paper compares a screening benchmark with two sequential games in which privately informed buyers either communicate preferences through cheap talk or signal them by requesting a product design. Equilibrium preference revelation is characterized as a separating perfect Bayesian equilibrium.

components.label: Separating perfect Bayesian equilibria under A-Learning and O-Learning
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Separating perfect Bayesian equilibria under A-Learning and O-Learning. Proposition 1 gives a necessary-and-sufficient type-heterogeneity threshold for truthful cheap talk under A-Learning. Proposition 3 gives the corresponding threshold for first-best self-design to separate types under O-Learning, supported by specified out-of-equilibrium beliefs. The appendix shows that the cheap-signaling outcome is the only separating equilibrium when it exists.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: The paper compares three regimes. In the screening benchmark, the seller posts a quality-price menu and buyers self-select. Under A-Learning, a buyer privately observes its type and sends a costless message, the seller chooses quality and incurs the selling cost, and the parties bargain over price. Under O-Learning, the informed buyer requests a quality, the seller accepts or rejects and incurs the selling cost if it accepts, and the parties then bargain over price.
